title: Sign-change deletion for orthogonal reflection words
statement: Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space [def-weil-vector-space-dimension] with a positive definite symmetric bilinear form $(\ ,\ )$. For $a\ne0$ write $s_a(x)=x-2(x,a)(a,a)^{-1}a$. Let $R\subseteq V\setminus\{0\}$ and $P\subseteq R$ satisfy $R=P\sqcup(-P)$. Let $D\subseteq P$ satisfy, for every $a\in D$, $s_a(R)=R$ and $s_a(P\setminus\{a\})=P\setminus\{a\}$. For $k\geq0$, $a_1,\ldots,a_k\in D$, and $b\in P$, set $w=s_{a_1}\cdots s_{a_k}$, with the rightmost factor acting first. If $wb\in-P$, then $k\geq1$ and there is $j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$ such that $$w s_b=s_{a_1}\cdots s_{a_{j-1}}s_{a_{j+1}}\cdots s_{a_k}.$$ No finiteness, spanning, integrality, or Coxeter-presentation assumption on $R$ is required.

source.place: Appendix C.10, printed p.610, exchange argument underlying freeness (the book refers to Humphreys 1990, 1.8); agent-formulated sign-partition version, without assuming a Coxeter presentation.

proof.text: For nonzero $a$, put $d=(a,a)>0$ and $\lambda_x=2(x,a)/d$. The formula $s_ax=x-\lambda_xa$ is linear, gives $s_aa=-a$ and $(s_ax,a)=-(x,a)$, hence $s_a^2x=x$. Bilinearity and symmetry give $$(s_ax,s_ay)=(x,y)-\lambda_y(x,a)-\lambda_x(a,y)+\lambda_x\lambda_y d=(x,y).$$ Thus every word of these reflections is a linear map preserving the form, including the empty word.

proof.text: If $q$ is such a word and $b\ne0$, then $(qb,qb)=(b,b)>0$, and substitution gives, for every $x$, $$q s_bx=qx-\frac{2(x,b)}{(b,b)}qb=qx-\frac{2(qx,qb)}{(qb,qb)}qb=s_{qb}qx.$$ Therefore $q s_b=s_{qb}q$. This is a calculation from the displayed formula, with no presentation of the reflection group assumed.

proof.text: Since $P\cap(-P)=\varnothing$, the empty word sends $b\in P$ into $P$, not into $-P$. Thus the hypothesis implies $k\geq1$. Define $c_{k+1}=b$ and $c_i=s_{a_i}\cdots s_{a_k}b$ for $1\leq i\leq k$. Each $c_i$ belongs to $R$ by repeated application of $s_{a_i}(R)=R$, so lies in exactly one of $P$ and $-P$. Since $c_1=wb\in-P$ and $c_{k+1}\in P$, choose the largest $j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$ with $c_j\in-P$. Maximality implies $c_{j+1}\in P$.

source.place: Appendix C.10, printed p.610 (PDF p.622), freeness/exchange input; agent-written details for the stated sign-partition generalization. Reflection formula as in C.8, printed p.609, and C.20, printed p.611.

proof.text: Now $c_j=s_{a_j}c_{j+1}$. If $c_{j+1}\ne a_j$, then $c_{j+1}\in P\setminus\{a_j\}$ and the stated equality $s_{a_j}(P\setminus\{a_j\})=P\setminus\{a_j\}$ puts $c_j$ in $P$, contradicting $c_j\in-P$. Consequently $c_{j+1}=a_j$. This uses only the sign-preservation hypothesis, not finiteness or a spanning property of $R$.

source.place: Appendix C.10, printed p.610 (PDF p.622), freeness/exchange input; agent-written details for the stated sign-partition generalization. Reflection formula as in C.8, printed p.609, and C.20, printed p.611.

proof.text: Set $p=s_{a_1}\cdots s_{a_{j-1}}$ and $q=s_{a_{j+1}}\cdots s_{a_k}$, allowing either to be empty. Then $qb=c_{j+1}=a_j$, so step 2 gives $q s_b=s_{a_j}q$. Using step 1, $$w s_b=p s_{a_j}q s_b=p s_{a_j}s_{a_j}q=pq=s_{a_1}\cdots s_{a_{j-1}}s_{a_{j+1}}\cdots s_{a_k}.$$ This is the required deletion at the index $1\leq j\leq k$.
